title: The American Town You Can Only Reach Through Canada
description: Point Roberts, Washington is a piece of the United States that you can only reach by driving through Canada. This is the strange true story of how a single line drawn in 1846 stranded an American town on the wrong side of the border, and what it reveals about how the modern map was really made.

scenes.t: Imagine living in the United States, but every time you want to visit the rest of your own country, you first have to leave it, driving through a foreign nation just to get back home.
scenes.img: cinematic aerial view of a small coastal town on a green peninsula at golden hour, calm sea, documentary, 16:9

scenes.t: For about a thousand Americans, this is not a thought experiment. It is ordinary, everyday life.
scenes.img: cinematic quiet small american town street, wooden houses, soft morning light, documentary, 16:9

scenes.t: This is Point Roberts, Washington. A small piece of the United States that hangs beneath Canada, cut off from the rest of America by land. To understand how this happened, we have to go back to a line drawn on a map in 1846.
scenes.img: cinematic map of the pacific northwest coastline showing a small peninsula below the 49th parallel border, dramatic lighting, 16:9

scenes.t: In the 1840s, the United States and Britain were locked in a bitter argument over where their western territories should divide. The two nations nearly went to war over it.
scenes.img: 1840s diplomats in a candlelit room negotiating over a large map, oil painting style, dramatic, 16:9

scenes.t: In 1846, they signed the Oregon Treaty. The solution seemed simple and clean. They would draw the border straight along the 49th parallel, all the way from the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific Ocean.
scenes.img: vintage 19th century map of north america with a long straight border line, sepia, cinematic, 16:9

scenes.t: But a straight line does not care about geography. And just below that line, a small peninsula reached quietly down from Canada into the sea.
scenes.img: satellite style view of a green peninsula crossing a straight border line into the ocean, dramatic, 16:9

scenes.t: The tip of that peninsula sat below the 49th parallel. By the letter of the treaty, it was American soil. But physically, it was attached only to Canada, and to nothing else American.
scenes.img: aerial of the forested tip of a peninsula with a faint border line cutting across it, surrounded by ocean, cinematic, 16:9

scenes.t: And so, almost by accident, Point Roberts was born. Five square miles of the United States, stranded on the wrong side of the border.
scenes.img: cinematic wooden welcome sign reading Point Roberts USA at golden hour, forest and sea behind, 16:9

scenes.t: To reach the rest of Washington State by road, a resident of Point Roberts must cross into Canada, drive about twenty five miles through British Columbia, then cross back into the United States. Two international borders, just to stay in their own country.
scenes.img: a car waiting at a US Canada border crossing booth, documentary photography, overcast, 16:9

scenes.t: For decades, this shaped every part of daily life. Children were bused across the border to attend school on the American mainland, crossing into Canada and back, twice a day, every single school day.
scenes.img: a yellow school bus at an international border crossing, cinematic documentary, 16:9

scenes.t: A trip to a big hospital, a license office, or a shopping mall could mean showing your passport four times in a single afternoon.
scenes.img: close up of a passport being handed to an officer at a border booth, documentary, 16:9

scenes.t: When the borders closed during the pandemic, Point Roberts became one of the most isolated communities in America. Water on three sides, and a sealed border on the fourth.
scenes.img: empty quiet small town street under grey overcast sky, lonely isolated mood, cinematic, 16:9

scenes.t: And yet, the strangeness has its rewards. Point Roberts is quiet, safe, and stunningly beautiful. Bald eagles nest in its trees, and orcas pass just offshore.
scenes.img: a bald eagle perched in a tall tree with a calm ocean behind, cinematic nature, 16:9

scenes.t: Its odd status even made it useful. Canadians rent mailboxes there to receive American packages, and its remoteness once made it a quiet place for people who simply wanted to disappear.
scenes.img: rows of mailboxes inside a small rural american post office, warm light, documentary, 16:9

scenes.t: But Point Roberts is more than a curiosity. It is a living reminder that the borders we treat as natural are often just lines that someone once drew. Lines that can trap a whole town on the wrong side, forever.
scenes.img: a long straight border clearing cutting through dense green forest to the horizon, aerial, dramatic, 16:9

scenes.t: All across the world, from Europe to Asia, similar accidents of geography have created enclaves, exclaves, and towns split between nations. Each one a small story of how the modern map was really made.
scenes.img: cinematic world map at night with several glowing points highlighted, dramatic, 16:9

scenes.t: The world is not drawn the way it is by nature. It is drawn by treaties, by wars, and by the occasional straight line that forgot to look at the ground. And that is history that explains the world.
scenes.img: cinematic view of planet earth from space with warm sunrise light on the horizon, 16:9
